title: 'Big Friendly Drone' will rain death on wilding pines
key_facts: SPS Automation (R&D in Christchurch, manufacturing in Timaru) showed the BFD 70 drone at the 2026 New Zealand Aerospace Summit.
It is 4.5 m across, weighs up to 160 kg at takeoff, carries up to 50 kg of spray and will cost about $150,000 when released early next year.
An Nvidia GPU, stereo cameras and lidar let its AI identify a wilding pine, estimate its size, spray a dose and move to the next.
It could clear a 5 sq km area, and one operator in Christchurch could remotely run several drones, stepping in only if things go wrong.
Its smaller predecessor, the AC-16, sprayed more than 400 wilding pines over 500 ha in a Central Otago trial in 2.5 days; the maker reports a 100% kill rate on return.
The government put wilding pine funding at $110 million over three years and plans to ease certification for large drones, aiming for new rules by mid-2027.
Wilding pines could cost over $5 billion in economic losses over 50 years, the government says.
quote_evidence: Its AI system, cameras and sensors will allow it to identify a wilding pine, estimate its size, spray the appropriate dose to kill it, then go in search of its next victim.
The idea is that one operator at a Christchurch mission control will be able to remotely wrangle multiple BFD 70s around the country.
Unchecked, they could cause more than $5 billion in economic losses over the next 50 years, the Government says.
why_it_matters_hint: Autonomous spraying drones could cut the time and cost of removing invasive pines, as NZ eases large-drone rules.
notes: Product shown at a summit, not yet released; performance and kill-rate figures come from the maker. Currency is presumably NZ dollars; the article does not say. Article is a Herald premium page, read in full.
